chunks: The ground loop in a measurement. The question: When measuring a signal, what is the ground loop?
When you measure with an oscilloscope (scope) probe, you connect two things: the tip to the signal and the ground lead to a ground point.
Together with the board's own return copper, these form a closed loop. That loop is part of the measurement.
It can ring after a fast edge and pick up noise, so what you see may not be what is really on the board.
Imagine holding a hula hoop up in the rain. The bigger the hoop, the more rain it catches.
A measuring loop catches stray magnetic fields from nearby switching wires in the same way, and bigger loops catch more. Now picture the loop as a long, springy rope.
A sudden jolt keeps it swinging for a while. A long ground lead behaves like that rope, ringing after each fast edge.
The probe presents its input capacitance C in to the node through the ground lead's inductance L lead (orange), and the scope displays V scope, the voltage across C in.
The loop is: source, tip, C in, L lead, board return and back to the source. A fast edge excites the LC resonance.
Loop: a closed path that current flows around, here made by the tip, the ground lead and the board return.
Return path: the route a signal's current takes back to where it started. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current. A longer wire has more.
Probe capacitance: the probe tip's small ability to store charge, around 10 picofarads (picofarads) for a typical probe.
Ringing: a signal wobbling back and forth after a fast edge.
A 15 cm clip lead has roughly 150 nanohenries.
With 10 picofarads of probe capacitance, the loop rings at about 130 megahertz, and a fast edge shows overshoot (the signal swinging past its true level) that is not on the board.
A short spring tip of roughly 10 nanohenries rings near 500 megahertz, far above most of the signal.
The phrase has a second meaning: a mains ground loop, which adds 50 or 60 hertz hum when the scope and the board both connect to earth through the wall-socket wiring.
That is the whole idea.
"The ground loop is the closed loop made by the probe tip, the signal path, the ground lead and the board's return path.
It has inductance, about 1 nanohenries per mm, which rings with the probe's capacitance, and it has area, which picks up magnetic fields.
It's part of the measurement, not just the board. Separately, 'ground loop' can mean multiple earth connections that carry current and inject mains hum."
Quick check. In probing, what is 'the ground loop'?
